text: Not every circuit that uses the same gates costs the same amount on real hardware. Two numbers, width and depth, capture the cost that actually matters, and this lesson defines both precisely and shows you how to count them by hand.

Width is simply the number of qubits a circuit uses — a strict admission requirement, since a 50-qubit circuit cannot run on a 20-qubit device no matter how shallow it is. Depth is subtler: it's not the total gate count, it's the length of the longest chain of gates that must happen in strict time order. Gates on completely disjoint qubits, no shared control or target, can share a layer and run in parallel. Gates that share any qubit cannot, because that qubit can only pass through one gate at a time.

Take a 3-qubit circuit: H on qubit 1, H on qubit 2, then CNOT with qubit 1 as control and qubit 2 as target, qubit 3 untouched. Width is 3, three wires, regardless of how many have active gates. Depth is 2: the two H gates act on disjoint qubits, so they share layer 1, but the CNOT needs both qubits' post-H states, so it can't join that layer and needs layer 2 of its own. Depth tracks dependency chains, not raw gate count.

On real hardware, every qubit is slowly losing quantum information to its environment, a process called decoherence, while also accumulating small gate-execution errors. Each sequential layer takes real time, and that's real time for noise to corrupt the state — a depth-50 circuit accumulates roughly ten times the noise exposure of a depth-5 circuit doing comparable work. That's exactly why compilers and transpilers, covered next lesson, work hard specifically to reduce depth, sometimes even using more gates overall if more of them can run in parallel.
Next lesson explains why real hardware only implements a small, fixed set of native gates, and how everything else gets rewritten in terms of them.
